interactions.label: A 50-year-old farmer presents to your PHC with diffuse body aches for three week

params.question: A 50-year-old farmer presents to your PHC with diffuse body aches for three weeks. Physical examination and basic investigations are normal. On systematic enquiry, he reports poor sleep, significant weight loss, inability to concentrate on his work, persistent fatigue, and complete loss of interest in farming — an activity he previously loved. He insists he is 'not sad, just tired.' Which of the following best explains whether this presentation meets the criteria for a major depressive episode?

answers.text: It does not, because the patient explicitly denies depressed mood, which is mandatory for diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DSM-5 requires depressed mood OR anhedonia — not both. Anhedonia (marked loss of interest or pleasure) can serve as the anchor symptom even when the patient denies feeling sad, which is common in masked depression.

answers.text: It does, because anhedonia serves as an anchor symptom in place of overt depressed mood, and he has five qualifying symptoms persisting beyond two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This patient has anhedonia (loss of interest in farming), insomnia, weight loss, poor concentration, and fatigue — five symptoms including one anchor — lasting three weeks. In Indian primary care, depression frequently presents with somatic complaints rather than overt sadness.

answers.text: It does not, because the predominant somatic complaint suggests a physical rather than psychiatric diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Somatic complaints like body aches are among the most common presentations of depression in Indian clinical practice — sometimes called masked depression. Normal investigations with persistent neurovegetative symptoms should prompt active screening for mood disturbance.

answers.text: It cannot be determined without a specialist psychiatric assessment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Major depressive disorder can and should be diagnosed at the primary-care level using standard ICD-11 or DSM-5 criteria. Specialist referral is indicated for severe, treatment-resistant, or high-risk cases — not for initial diagnosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the two anchor symptoms: depressed mood and anhedonia. DSM-5 requires at least one of these plus a total of five symptoms for two weeks. In India, depression often presents with physical complaints rather than overt sadness — always screen.
Well done. Recognising anhedonia as a stand-alone anchor symptom, and screening for depression behind somatic complaints, are essential skills for Indian primary-care practice.

interactions.label: A patient starting an SSRI should be counselled that no benefit is possible unti

params.question: A patient starting an SSRI should be counselled that no benefit is possible until reuptake inhibition begins at two to four weeks.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. SSRI-induced reuptake inhibition begins within hours, not weeks. The clinical lag is due to slower downstream processes — increased BDNF and synaptic remodelling — that take two to four weeks. The drug is working at the receptor level from day one, but the brain needs time to structurally adapt.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Reuptake inhibition actually begins within hours of the first dose. The two-to-four-week delay in clinical improvement is attributed to downstream neuroplasticity changes, including increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and synaptic remodelling, not to delayed drug action at the synapse.

interactions.label: Which of the following correctly distinguishes hypomania from a full manic episo

params.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes hypomania from a full manic episode?

answers.text: Hypomania lasts at least four days with no major functional impairment and never includes psychotic features, whereas mania lasts at least one week and may include psychosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Hypomania is milder: symptoms persist for at least four days, cause no marked functional impairment, and never include psychotic features. A full manic episode requires at least one week (or any duration if hospitalisation is needed), typically causes significant disruption, and may feature grandiose or paranoid delusions.

answers.text: Hypomania is characterised by depressed mood, while mania involves elevated mood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both hypomania and mania feature elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy. Depression is the opposite pole in bipolar disorder, not a defining feature of hypomania.

answers.text: Hypomania requires more associated symptoms than mania for diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DSM-5 requires three or more associated features for both hypomania and mania (four if mood is only irritable). The key distinctions are duration, severity of impairment, and the presence or absence of psychotic features — not symptom count.

answers.text: Hypomania can include psychotic features provided the patient is not hospitalised

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Psychotic features never occur in hypomania — their presence automatically upgrades the diagnosis to a full manic episode. Hospitalisation status affects the duration criterion for mania, not the boundary between hypomania and mania.

overallFeedback.feedback: Hypomania differs from mania in three key ways: shorter minimum duration (4 days vs 1 week), no major functional impairment, and no psychotic features. These distinctions determine whether you refer urgently or manage conservatively.
Well done. This distinction is clinically critical: a manic episode, especially with psychotic features, demands urgent specialist referral, while hypomania may be managed more conservatively.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman with a history of one previous depressive episode is prescri

params.question: A 30-year-old woman with a history of one previous depressive episode is prescribed fluoxetine by her GP. Two weeks later, she presents with euphoria, decreased need for sleep, and grandiose plans to start three businesses simultaneously. Which of the following best explains this clinical scenario?

answers.text: Fluoxetine caused serotonin syndrome, which can present with euphoria and hyperactivity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serotonin syndrome presents with altered mental status, autonomic instability, and neuromuscular signs (hyperreflexia, clonus) — not sustained euphoria, grandiosity, and goal-directed hyperactivity. The clinical picture here is mania, not serotonergic toxicity.

answers.text: Antidepressant monotherapy can trigger a manic switch in patients with underlying bipolar disorder, suggesting her previous depressive episode was part of a bipolar spectrum illness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Antidepressant-induced mania is a well-documented phenomenon occurring when a patient with unrecognised bipolar disorder receives antidepressant monotherapy without a mood stabiliser. This highlights the importance of screening for prior hypomanic or manic symptoms before prescribing antidepressants.

answers.text: Fluoxetine at standard doses commonly causes transient euphoria that resolves spontaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SSRIs do not cause euphoria as a routine side effect. Early activation or restlessness can occur, but sustained euphoria with grandiosity and decreased need for sleep indicates a manic episode — not a self-limiting drug side effect.

answers.text: Her symptoms represent a normal rebound response to feeling better after weeks of depression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Recovery from depression involves a gradual return to baseline functioning, not sudden euphoria, grandiosity, and reckless planning. These symptoms constitute a manic episode requiring urgent reassessment, discontinuation of the antidepressant, and likely initiation of a mood stabiliser.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a patient develops mania shortly after starting an antidepressant, the most likely explanation is antidepressant-induced manic switch in unrecognised bipolar disorder. Screen for prior hypomania before prescribing, and never use antidepressant monotherapy in known bipolar disorder.
Well analysed. Always screen for a history of elevated mood episodes before prescribing antidepressants. Antidepressant monotherapy in unrecognised bipolar disorder is a preventable cause of mania.

interactions.label: A 35-year-old woman achieves full remission of her first episode of moderate dep

params.question: A 35-year-old woman achieves full remission of her first episode of moderate depression after eight weeks of sertraline. She feels well and wants to stop medication. What is the most appropriate recommendation?

answers.text: Discontinue sertraline immediately, since full remission indicates recovery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Remission is not the same as cure. The risk of relapse is highest in the months immediately following remission, which is why continuation therapy is recommended — stopping now significantly increases the chance of another episode.

answers.text: Continue sertraline for six to nine months after remission to prevent relapse, then taper gradually under supervision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. After a first episode, continuation therapy for six to nine months consolidates recovery and reduces relapse risk. Patients with two or more prior episodes need maintenance therapy for at least two years, and some require indefinite treatment.

answers.text: Halve the dose for two weeks and then stop, as gradual reduction is sufficient after eight weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Eight weeks is the time needed to achieve remission, not the continuation period. Tapering this early — regardless of how gradually — leaves the patient at high risk of relapse. The full therapeutic dose should be maintained for six to nine months after remission.

answers.text: Continue sertraline indefinitely, as all patients with depression require lifelong medication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lifelong treatment is not necessary for all patients. After a first episode, six to nine months of continuation therapy is standard. Extended maintenance of two years or longer is reserved for recurrent depression (two or more episodes) or other high-risk features.

overallFeedback.feedback: After remission of a first depressive episode, continue the antidepressant at full dose for six to nine months before considering a gradual supervised taper. For recurrent episodes, maintenance therapy of two years or longer is recommended.
Well done. Premature discontinuation is one of the most common causes of relapse. Counsel patients that feeling better is a reason to continue treatment, not to stop it.
